spatial_entity.notes: Historical polity identity aligned to Seshat gh_ashanti_emp, which records the Ashanti Empire from 1701 to 1895 and Asante as an alternative name. The attached Kumasi point is navigation only, not the polity or practice extent.

claim.date_text_original: Austin's specialist synthesis covers Asante slavery and pawnship, 1807-1896; normalized here to the independently reviewed polity interval ending 1895.
claim.spatial_precision: Asante polity-level specialist synthesis; not uniformity at every locality
claim.summary: Specialist economic history concludes that slavery and slave trading were widespread in nineteenth-century Asante and that enslaved labour was a major input across productive activities. The atlas records slavery as a reviewed polity-level practice in Asante from 1807 through the end of the independent Ashanti Empire in 1895, while keeping pawnship as a distinct coercive institution rather than merging it into the slavery category.
claim.notes: This is a broad period-level synthesis, not an inference from archive counts or a single event. Austin's chapter also treats pawnship; this claim does not collapse pawns into enslaved status. No P-level or population share is assigned.

territorial_practice.notes: Supports polity-level presence and widespread institutional use during the reviewed period without asserting uniform local prevalence or deriving intensity from source density.

source.title: Labour, Land and Capital in Ghana: From Slavery to Free Labour in Asante, 1807-1956
source.temporal_scope: 1807-1956, with precolonial slavery/pawnship analysis focused on 1807-1896
source.independence_notes: Major specialist economic-history synthesis drawing on archival, ethnographic and historical evidence. Internal citations are not counted as independent attestations merely because they are numerous.
source.reliability_limitations: Treats several forms of coerced and dependent labour. Slavery, slave trading and pawnship must remain analytically distinct; chapter-level statements do not imply identical practice at every locality.

version.version_label: Boydell & Brewer / University of Rochester Press, print 2005; chapter 8, pp. 155-170

evidence.evidence_role: principal specialist synthesis for polity-level slavery classification
evidence.locator: Chapter 8, pp. 155-170, especially the opening synthesis stating that slavery, slave trading and pawning were widespread in nineteenth-century Asante and major inputs into productive activities.
evidence.notes: Use the slavery-specific proposition for this claim. Pawnship remains a separate category.

source.title: Accumulation, wealth and belief in Asante history: I. To the close of the nineteenth century
source.temporal_scope: Asante to the close of the nineteenth century
source.independence_notes: Independent specialist interpretation of Asante social and economic history; used as contextual corroboration rather than a second prevalence count.
source.reliability_limitations: The article's primary purpose is wealth, accumulation and belief, not a dedicated quantitative history of slavery.

evidence.locator: pp. 23-43; Asante accumulation, social formation and labour/wealth context.
evidence.notes: Context only; the Austin monograph remains the principal classification source.

The point is used only as a navigation proxy until an exact pinned Cliopatria polity row is frozen; it is not the slavery inference extent or a substitute for the historical Asante boundary.
